bridge: Builds on N04 transport and N02 routing. Resolve only documentation names on paper; no mail sending is required.
teaching:
DNS maps names to typed records through a hierarchy and caches. A client typically asks a recursive resolver, which may query authoritative servers or use cached data. TTL limits cache lifetime under the protocol; it is not a promise that the service address never changes.

A records carry IPv4 addresses, AAAA IPv6, CNAME aliases and MX mail routing information. Resolution supplies data about a name; it does not by itself authenticate an HTTPS application. DNSSEC can authenticate signed DNS data under its trust chain, but it is distinct from encrypting the transport to a resolver.

Email combines routing, transfer and message interpretation. SPF, DKIM and DMARC address particular sending-domain/authentication policies; they do not prove every message claim is true or safe to act on. A displayed friendly sender name is not a verified identity. Evaluate the actual domain, authentication results, requested action and independent context.

DNS record types answer different questions: A gives an IPv4 address, AAAA gives an IPv6 address, and MX names a mail exchanger whose address is resolved separately. A recursive resolver commonly answers the client and makes iterative upstream queries; authoritative root/TLD servers do not normally recurse for the client. Cached TTLs reduce repeated work but make changes non-instantaneous. For email, distinguish SMTP server relay (port 25) from client submission (commonly 587, or 465 with implicit TLS) and IMAP retrieval. The SMTP envelope and visible From/To headers can differ. Modern message formats, MIME and negotiated extensions go beyond the legacy ASCII-only teaching model; TLS protection also needs an explicit endpoint and validation policy.
example:
Invented zone:
notes.example. 300 IN A 192.0.2.10
www.example.   300 IN CNAME notes.example.
example.       300 IN MX 10 mail.example.
mail.example.  300 IN A 192.0.2.20

At t=0 resolver caches notes.example with TTL300.
At t=120 remaining lifetime is about180 seconds.
explanation: The alias points to another DNS name rather than directly to an address. The MX preference10 is a routing priority value, not a port. A cached result can remain visible until expiry even after an authoritative update. The .example names are reserved teaching data.
exercise: Using the records above, trace lookup of www.example through its alias to an IPv4 address. Calculate remaining TTL at t=250. Explain why successful lookup does not establish that an email claiming to be from support is legitimate.
solution: The address is 192.0.2.10 and remaining TTL is about50 seconds in this simplified cache. DNS resolution is not verification of a human sender or the content of a request.
challenge: Classify the purpose of AAAA, MX and CNAME. A message passes domain authentication but asks you to reveal a password. Explain what the authentication result does and does not establish, without sending or opening any message attachment.
challenge_solution: AAAA supplies IPv6 data; MX mail routing; CNAME an alias. Domain authentication can support a domain-level provenance/policy claim; it does not establish benign content, uncompromised sender intent or authorisation to request secrets.
